_what: The shared behaviour of Crow's clients, declared by hand. tools/check_shared_core.py holds every surface against this file.
_why_written_by_hand: A list generated from cli/crow_core.py shrinks with its input: the day a behaviour LEAVES the core, the expected list loses it too and the checker stays green. This list is the promise, the core is the evidence, and they are allowed to disagree. Keys starting with _ are documentation, the same convention manifests/operating-point.json uses.
_two_classes: names/ carries things with a def, a class or a module binding behind them - four predicates apply. wordings/ carries user-visible sentences and literal values, which have no def name at all - the counting predicate from #90's E2 applies: written once, and that once in the core. The split exists because the first draft of this manifest listed the three refusal sentences under the def predicates, where nothing could ever check them while the tool printed 'all'.

_not_listed_and_why.sampling triple: temperature 1.0 / top_p 0.95 / min_p 0.01 belongs to manifests/operating-point.json, and tools/check_operating_point.py already counts it across every client source. Typing 0.95 in here would create a THIRD written copy of the number - the exact drift both checkers exist to prevent - and this one would be the copy no measurement reads.
_not_listed_and_why.next_context_tokens as a user entry: the counting is wired transitively: run_turn returns the number in TurnResult.context_tokens and the surface only draws it. Demanding a direct call site in every surface would be red at a correctly wired client.
_not_listed_and_why.the three thought events themselves: reasoning_started/reasoning_text/reasoning_finished are methods of ReplyEvents, not module-level names, and the four predicates anchor at column 0 or at an indented def of the DECLARED name. ReasoningBlocks below is the entry that carries them: it is the only thing that fires them, and a surface that does not implement them fails its user_entry evidence.

surfaces.label: gui
surfaces.why: The window, and since #187 the only client: the terminal client cli/crow.py was removed, so the window is the client. Until it landed the core had ONE consumer (the terminal) and a green result here was the tool measuring itself; since #187 it is one consumer again, and the honesty rule asks for at least one declared surface plus the helpers held to predicates (1)-(3). It owns widgets, the tick and the German surface language; it owns no decision. It lives in cli/ and not gui/ because tools/pack-release.ps1:431 copies cli/ as a whole and nothing else, so a gui/ would be absent from the package with nothing saying so.

helpers.label: platform
helpers.why: The one module that knows which operating system this is: paths (XDG on Linux, %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows), process discovery, spawn flags, the kill, the shell, the browser list, the font store and the updater command. A HELPER and not a surface, because it is not a client of the core -- it decides nothing a user can see, it answers WHERE and HOW. It is held to the definition and import predicates like every helper: a platform file that started carrying a refusal, a wording or a release level would be a second core, and that is exactly the drift this manifest exists to catch. It may not import crow_core (the core imports IT), so a core name appearing in here is a finding rather than a wiring. The name is crow_platform and never platform: cli/ is on sys.path[0] for every client started from this directory, and cli/platform.py would shadow the standard library module of that name.

helpers.label: voice
helpers.why: Dictation: the microphone and the recogniser, and nothing else. A HELPER and not a surface, because it is not a client of the core -- it owns audio and the text that comes out of it, never a turn, a prompt or a session. It is still held to the definition and import predicates: if it ever re-decided something crow_core.py already decides, that is exactly the drift this manifest exists to catch. It lives in cli/ for the reason crow_gui.py gives -- tools/pack-release.ps1 copies cli/ as a whole and nothing else -- and beside the window because only the window can reach it: the terminal has no button to press.

helpers.label: remote
helpers.why: #249, the phone's way into a running window: a LAN-only HTTP server (pairing, paired devices, the /api dispatcher, the event streams) and the QR encoder for its pairing URL. A HELPER and not a surface, because it is not a client of the core -- it owns transport and pairing, never a turn, a wording or a decision: the /remote wording lives in the core, every call it forwards is answered by the window's Api, and what reaches it are callables. It never imports crow_core, so a core name appearing in here is a finding rather than a wiring. Its own status lines go to crow.log through a callable, not into the chat. It lives in cli/ for the reason crow_gui.py gives -- tools/pack-release.ps1 copies cli/ as a whole and nothing else.

helpers.label: boot
helpers.why: #196 phase 1, the boot menu: starts one of the three operating points from manifests/stack.json (serve, and sd-server for the Image Stack), waits for readiness, writes the contract file and opens the window against it. A HELPER and not a surface, because it is not a client of the core -- it never runs a turn, a session or a tool; it is a launcher that starts processes and then the surface. Every core fact it needs (the contract file, the point a serve is, the process scan, the image server's working folder) it takes from crow_core by qualified name, so a second definition here is exactly what predicates (1)-(3) catch. It lives in cli/ for the reason crow_gui.py gives -- tools/pack-release.ps1 copies cli/ as a whole and nothing else.

helpers.label: boot-gui
helpers.why: #196, the operating-point window: the boot menu as a window (`crow_boot.py --gui`, the shortcut's target under pythonw.exe), with its page in cli/crow_boot_gui.html. A HELPER and not a surface, for the reason crow_boot.py is one: it never runs a turn, a session or a tool. It is a face over crow_boot.Boot and decides nothing of its own -- the plan, the one-at-a-time check, the start, the readiness wait, the contract file, Stop and Start Crow are Boot's, called as they are; it holds only the window's state and wording. The one core fact it shows itself (the crow-nest port) it takes from crow_core by qualified name, so a core name defined in here is a finding. The crow on its taskbar button is the window's own icon code (crow_gui.shell_buttons, crow_gui.icon_png), imported when the window opens rather than copied; only its AppUserModelID is its own. It lives in cli/ for the reason crow_gui.py gives -- tools/pack-release.ps1 copies cli/ as a whole and nothing else.

names.name: tool_read_file
names.why: The read half of the read-before-write rule. A second implementation would populate a different _READ and the refusal would stop matching the reads that earned it.

names.name: tool_read_image
names.why: #170. The one reader that hands back an image block instead of text, and the only place that decides what counts as an image on the wire. A second copy would answer 'which formats' differently from image_part's table, and the surface with the older answer would refuse a file the other one sends.

names.name: tool_render_page
names.why: #175. The only place that starts a browser, and the only one that owns the handle it kills. A second copy would sweep by name sooner or later -- that is exactly the mistake #158 paid for once -- and it would answer differently about where a render lands, which is the boundary read_image then has to obey.

names.name: tool_generate_image
names.why: #300 phase 3. The only place that talks to the image server and owns the handle that stops it. A second copy would start a second sd-server beside the first, and 29.8 GB of weights would sit in RAM twice.

names.name: tool_edit_image
names.why: #300 phase 3. The two-stage edit robin chose on the pictures (1 MP edit, then img2img at full size). A second copy would drift back to a 4 MP edit, which measured grainy (E1, E2).

names.name: tool_animate_image
names.why: #340. The only place that moves the card between the language model and ComfyUI (use_mode) around a clip, and always brings the language model back. A second copy would start ComfyUI beside the engine, and a clip alone peaked at 32,049 of 32,607 MiB in Phase 0.

names.name: tool_write_file
names.why: The one tool whose drift costs data: #10 measured hermes-agent resolving read-before-write to last-write-wins in two independent code paths, one warning and one writing anyway. Two implementations here is that same defect with a different name.

names.name: tool_append_file
names.why: The one write that carries no read guard, because appending destroys nothing -- and the only thing standing between it and a file outside the working area is the _outside_root check it shares with write_file. A second copy is where that check gets dropped, or where the missing trailing newline is handled differently and two rounds run together on one line.

names.name: tool_edit_file
names.why: Exact match plus a uniqueness check. A copy that fuzzy-matches instead would silently edit the wrong occurrence in whichever surface carries it.

names.name: tool_list_dir
names.why: One of the seven. Its result goes through _clip, and a copy that forgot that ceiling would put an unbounded directory listing into the prefill.

names.name: tool_find_files
names.why: Carries both ceilings - hit count AND bytes - because either alone lets the other through. A second copy is where one of the two gets dropped.

names.name: tool_search_text
names.why: The tool that cost eight minutes of prefill when only the hit count was capped. The measurement behind the byte ceiling lives with this function, not with its callers.

names.name: tool_run_command
names.why: Local execution with a timeout and a secret-stripped environment. A surface that ships its own would be shipping its own idea of what a child process may see.

names.name: tool_build_bundle
names.why: #212. The one place that decides which esbuild runs (project node_modules, PATH, then the runtime caches) and how a module graph becomes one offline page. A second copy would find a different bundler, or inline a module script as a classic one in <head> where the canvas does not exist yet.

names.name: tool_git_status
names.why: #156. The repository a surface reports on is the one the WORKING AREA is bound to, never the process's cwd -- the window's cwd is whatever the shortcut handed it. A surface with its own copy would be a surface with its own idea of which repository it is looking at.

names.name: tool_git_diff
names.why: #156. Runs a fixed argv with no shell, so a path that looks like an option stays a path. That guarantee is the reason the git group exists instead of `run_command "git diff ..."`, and it has to hold in both surfaces.

names.name: tool_git_log
names.why: #156. The unit-separator format and the 50-row ceiling live here: a commit subject may contain a comma, a pipe and a tab, and a surface parsing its own log would be a surface that reports somebody's subject line as three fields.

names.name: tool_git_commit
names.why: #156. It stages EXACTLY the paths it was given -- no -a, no dot -- and passes the message as one argument rather than through a shell. Both are safety rules, not conveniences: a second copy is where the sweep-everything version appears, and where PS 5.1 breaks a message that starts a line with `--` again.

names.name: tool_git_push
names.why: #156. The one call that leaves the machine, and robins Ansage vom 2026-08-29 is that it asks every time. It records the event for the panel's history as well -- a push is not in any git log, so a surface with its own push would be a surface whose history is missing what it did.

names.name: tool_github_connect
names.why: #156. The device flow is one implementation because the token store is one file: a surface that ran its own flow would write its own token, and 'connected' would mean something different in the window than in the terminal. It also never blocks for the fifteen minutes the code is valid -- that decision belongs to the core, not to whoever draws the code.

names.name: tool_web_search
names.why: #96. The entry point of web research, and the only place the wording that stops a turn ending in a list of links is written. A surface with its own copy would be a surface with its own idea of what counts as an answer -- and of how many pages one question may cost.

names.name: tool_fetch_url
names.why: #96. One page, as text, with extraction ahead of the clip. It is here rather than in a surface because the two rules it carries are core rules: http(s) only, so it cannot become a disk read around #92's boundary, and every failure comes back as a tool result rather than an exception.

names.name: tool_memory
names.why: #120. The two memory stores are written through one function because BOTH surfaces have to fill the same files: a terminal that saved to one place and a window that saved to another would be two memories for one user. The bounds live here too -- the limit that refuses instead of trimming, the duplicate that answers success, the injection scan -- because every one of them is a rule about what may enter the system prompt, and the system prompt is the core's.

names.name: tool_skill
names.why: #124. Skills are global and both surfaces read the same directory, so the file format, the frontmatter and the enabled flag are core rules -- a window that spelled `enabled` differently from the terminal would show a skill as on while the prompt left it out. The read action lives here for the same reason the memory tool has none: what is in the head is decided here, and a skill body is deliberately not in it.

names.name: tool_session_search
names.why: #123. The FTS5 index is derived from the chat files, so it must be built by whoever can see all of them -- which is the core, not a surface. A second builder in the window would index a different set the first time either side changed where a chat is written.

names.name: tool_delegate
names.why: #143. The fan-out is one registry in one process: a surface that started its own threads would race the core's on the delegate spot, the subtask ids and the transcript folder. The rule it enforces -- the local slot is never a delegation target -- is a core rule, not a window preference.

names.name: tool_subtasks
names.why: #143. The listing reads the same registry `delegate` writes; a surface with its own idea of subtask state would show running where the core says done.

names.name: tool_collect
names.why: #143. The blocking wait owns the two doors out -- the INTERRUPT flag it must never consume and the deadline that turns a stalled provider into a sentence. Two waiters would be two answers to who gets the Ctrl+C.

names.name: tool_goal_set
names.why: #165. The plan the model writes for itself. One writer, because goal.json is the one record that outlives a rollover, a reboot and a new session (#163): a second surface writing its own shape there would hand the recovery a file it cannot read.

names.name: tool_goal_step
names.why: #165. The one door that moves a step, and since #168 the one that reopens a finished one. Two implementations would be two answers to what a tick means -- and the engine picks the first step that is not done, so a second answer sends it past the work that is running.

names.name: tool_judge
names.why: #266. The fresh-eyes judge of a capture: one spot order (judge pin, delegate chain, own model in a fresh request), one rubric order (accept lines, PLAN.md, caller, default) and one place the verdict lands on the goal step, where goal_step's gate (#267) reads it. A second implementation would be a second answer to who judged and against what.

names.name: subtask_view
names.why: #143 E2. The one list every surface draws the delegation state from -- cards, rail children and the chip all read it. A surface with its own idea of subtask state shows running where the registry says done.

names.name: cancel_subtasks
names.why: #143 E2. Stop reaches the subtasks through this and nothing else: the mark promises the record -- result dropped, no transcript, status interrupted -- because a socket read cannot be torn out from under its thread.

names.name: TOOL_IMPL
names.why: The name-to-function table. It is a dict rather than a def, which is why the manifest needs a kind at all: hanging a def predicate on it would declare it and check nothing. A second table is how one surface ends up offering six tools and the other seven.

names.name: run_tool
names.why: EVERY FAILURE IS A RESULT, NOT AN EXCEPTION. A tool that raises kills the turn and costs the whole prefix; at ~10 tok/s that is minutes. A second dispatcher is where the try/except gets lost.

names.name: run_tool_cached
names.why: The repeat cache that turned an eight-attempt loop on a non-existent path into a fact the model has to react to. A surface without it loops; a surface with its own copy loops differently.

names.name: format_tool_args
names.why: #99. The one line a tool call is rendered as, on both surfaces. It lived in cli/crow.py while cli/crow_gui.py reached for crow_core.format_tool_args behind a hasattr guard that had been False since the split -- so the window showed raw JSON where the terminal showed values, and nothing could detect it because the name was not declared here.

names.name: restore_root
names.why: #92. What the window binds at start, and the three states it has to tell apart: no key at all (nobody ever chose), an explicit null (somebody chose 'no folder', and that survives a restart too), and a path that may since have stopped being a root. A surface with its own version would collapse the first two and an explicit 'no folder' would come back as a folder on the next start.

names.name: set_active_root

only.because: The terminal must NOT write it, and that is the entry rather than a comment: `--root` states where THAT run works, while `active` decides where the WINDOW opens next time. They were nearly one key -- `recent[0]` -- and `crow --root D:\x` in a terminal would then have silently moved the window's next start. The terminal client went with #187; the line stays so a second surface that writes it goes red.

names.why: #92. Written only where a person chose: the picker, or 'no folder'. `remember_root` fills the menu and is a different fact -- both surfaces write that one.

names.name: mandated_paths
names.why: #98, and it is what makes the boundary usable rather than obstructive: a path the USER named is released, a path the assistant picked is not. Written once because a surface with its own idea of what counts as an instruction would refuse things its user typed -- the exact failure #98 recorded, where an explicit 'Erstell die Datei C:\Users\robin\Desktop\x.txt' was refused and the model then reported for obeying it. It reads `user` messages only; counting the assistant's own text would let the model widen its permission by mentioning a path first.

names.name: escaped_the_working_area
names.why: #98. Whether a shell command ran in a turn the boundary already refused -- the sequence the working-area guarantee does NOT cover, stated once so both surfaces mark the same event. A surface with its own version would drift into path matching against a shell string, which is the analysis #98 rejected on the record.
names._evidence_note: The method, not the predicate: no surface CALLS escaped_the_working_area -- run_turn does, and hands the answer down as boundary_escaped. A surface's wiring is therefore the event it implements. A surface that skips it shows the user nothing when the working area is left, which is the whole defect #98 recorded.

names.name: _clip
names.why: Every tool result goes through here, no exceptions - one ceiling measured in the thing it actually costs, bytes that become prefill.

names.name: _post_stream
names.why: The SSE reader. Two of them means two ideas about what a delta is, and the reasoning/content split rides on that.

names.name: stream_reply
names.why: One request, one stream, one reasoning/content state machine. This is the name a GUI is most likely to re-implement, because a terminal-shaped signature looks like a terminal's business.

names.name: ReasoningBlocks
names.why: #90's capability 2, and its failure point P3: THE MODEL CAN RE-ENTER REASONING MID-ANSWER, so where a thought block begins, ends and begins again is a decision, not an order. The terminal shows and hides a block, the window folds and unfolds one - two presentations of ONE decision, and a second copy of it puts answer text inside a collapsed block where nobody reads it. The evidence is the event, because a surface that never draws a block is the second half of #90's failure: the CLI could not show reasoning at all until E10, and a window that could would have made it second-class on the day it shipped.
names._evidence_note: reasoning_started( rather than the class name: no surface CALLS ReasoningBlocks - stream_reply builds it - so a surface's wiring shows up as the block events it implements, not as a construction.

names.name: CodeFences

only.because: #90's capability 6 splits into two halves - WHERE a code block begins and ends, which is a decision, and how it is drawn with a copy button, which is a surface. This is the first half, and today only the window is wired to it. The terminal client carried its own fence handling in its Renderer until #187 removed it. The 'only' line stays so a second surface has to be wired to this class or declared here.

names.why: Two clients with two ideas of what a fence is means one frames what the other reads as prose. The rule this class carries and the Renderer does not: a fence is a WHOLE line, so 'call it with ```json' mid-sentence opens nothing, and what follows the backticks has to be a bare language tag.

names.name: run_turn
names.why: The tool loop and its four rules. Every surface runs turns, so every surface has to run THIS one: the rule about appending an assistant turn without its tool_calls has no visible effect inside the turn that breaks it, only in every later turn against the same prefix.

names.name: save_session
names.why: #90's capability 5, 'conversation history that survives a restart'. Both halves - the server's KV and the client's messages - or neither, and a surface that writes its own half writes a session the other cannot read.

names.name: load_session
names.why: The other end of the same file. A surface that does not wire it starts cold every time and nothing on screen says why.

names.name: Conversation
names.why: The append-only context. Nothing is ever inserted in front of, or edited inside, an existing message - the prompt cache only survives while the prefix stays byte-identical, and a re-prefill of 12k tokens costs minutes here.

names.name: next_context_tokens
names.why: How full the window is after a turn, asked of the server rather than estimated. The version that added prompt_n to predicted_n ran the bar BACKWARDS, 4.7k -> 1.3k -> 792, while the conversation grew.

names.name: TurnCost
names.why: #90's capability 7, tok/s and tokens per turn. Its FIELDS AND THEIR ORDER are the shared part: two surfaces that assemble the same six numbers into two different sentences are two products. The surface picks the colour and nothing else.

names.name: TurnResult
names.why: What one turn leaves behind - context_tokens, promised_warm, rolled. Those were local variables of repl() that the loop wrote through; a surface that carries them itself resumes against numbers that stopped being true.

names.name: start_server
names.why: The one place that turns a model key into a running server. Written twice it would be two command lines, and a fourth copy of the operating point is exactly what manifests/operating-point.json exists to prevent -- three copies already drifted once, on 2026-08-10. NO LONGER A USER ENTRY since #187: the terminal client that called it directly (#114) is gone, and the window reaches a server through `model_command` (#115) -- a DIRECT call site in cli/crow_gui.py would be a second boot path, and two llama-servers overbook the card without a word.

names.name: model_command
names.why: #115. Which models exist, how a typo is refused, and whether a switch happened at all. Both surfaces offer it -- `/model` in the terminal, the chip's menu in the window -- and a surface with its own version would be a second answer to 'may I do this now' and a second sentence about the lost context. #99 is the precedent for the cost: `format_tool_args` sat behind a hasattr guard that had been False since the split, so the command worked in one client and not the other, for months, with nothing able to see it.

names.name: reasoning_command
names.why: #116. Which thinking levels this model takes, how a typo is refused, and whether the change is worth a prefill. Both surfaces offer it -- `/reasoning` in the terminal, the slider in the window -- and the slider does not set the level, it types the command, for the reason #99 records: a control wired separately from the command it duplicates works in one client and not the other, and nothing in the suite can see it. The refusal is the load-bearing half: an invalid level does not fail here, it fails on the server AFTER the prefill has been paid for.

names.name: reasoning_for_chat
names.why: #116's third state. A level bound under one model is not necessarily one the next takes -- `max` is fine for 0731 and raises against unsloth's template -- so a stored value outside this model's list is treated as never chosen AND said. Two surfaces with two answers here is a chat that silently stopped doing what its own setting says. It also owns the rule that the invalid value is NOT written back: the user may return to the model it was valid for.

names.name: mode_description
names.why: The line that says what a level holds back. Both surfaces built it themselves until 2026-08-24, and both built it the same wrong way -- joining every name that asks. That is readable for twelve built-ins and becomes ninety lines the moment an MCP server arrives; robin hit it with higgsfield's 73. A second copy would drift the moment one surface learns to count and the other does not.

names.name: Unreachable
names.why: Nothing answered at the endpoint, as a TYPE rather than a text match on 'cannot reach'. It decides who gets told to start the server, so a surface that re-derived it from the message would hand that advice to a failed boot or a refused schema -- the distinction ServerBootError already exists for, one step further down.

names.name: failure_line
names.why: What a person reads when a turn died. Measured 2026-08-24: the advice was first written into the window's `except CrowError`, three cases went green, and the live window still printed the bare WinError -- `run_turn` reports a failed turn through `turn_failed` and never raises it, so that `except` is the rarer door. Two surfaces deciding this separately is how one of them ends up silent again.

wordings.why: The first of the three refusals with teeth. Its failure mode is losing work the model cannot see, so a second surface writing its own wording is a second surface deciding its own rule.

wordings.text: before editing it, in this conversation
wordings.why: The second refusal. The words 'in this conversation' are the scope #215-H decided (E6's 'in this turn' before it); a copy that says 'first' describes a rule nobody implemented.

wordings.id: a read file changed on disk
wordings.text: it changed on disk since you read it
wordings.why: #215-H. The refusal write_file and edit_file share when the file no longer carries the (mtime_ns, size) it was read with. A surface with its own wording would be a surface with its own idea of what 'read' still means.

wordings.text: include more context to make it unique
wordings.why: The third refusal. It fails loudly instead of guessing, and the sentence is what tells the model how to fix its own call.

wordings.text: narrow the query and ask again
wordings.why: The ceiling notice. If a surface writes its own, the two clients disagree about what a truncated result looks like to the model.

wordings.id: a repeat is answered from the first call
wordings.why: The sentence that turns a loop into a fact. Observed 2026-08-09: eight attempts at the same missing path, twice inside one round.

wordings.text: error: arguments were not valid JSON
wordings.why: Half of run_tool's contract, in the shape the model actually sees it. A raise here costs the whole prefix.

wordings.id: an unknown tool is a result
wordings.why: The other half, and the one that lists what IS available - a surface with its own list would advertise its own tool table.

wordings.id: loop rule: unanswerable calls are not appended
wordings.why: The rule with no visible effect inside the turn that breaks it. An assistant turn whose tool_calls have no tool message behind them is a broken prefix for every LATER turn of the session, and a probe is what found the first missing half of it.

wordings.id: loop rule: the budget buys rounds, not the turn
wordings.text: The tool budget for this turn is spent
wordings.why: Driven live with --max-tool-rounds 0 the model produced 102 tokens, 'thinking 100%', and the user was shown nothing. The extra round is what spends the rest on saying where things stood.
What the fresh conversation opens with after a mid-turn archive. Two wordings would be two answers to 'where did my context go'.

wordings.id: loop rule: a second rollover stops the turn
wordings.why: Twice in one turn means the question itself does not fit. Rolling again would archive the note and ask the same thing again, forever.

wordings.id: session format: the kv token count
wordings.why: The field the restore checks itself against. A second writer of session.json is a second schema, and the file is shared between surfaces by design.

What decides whether a restored KV cache belongs to the conversation being resumed. Computed differently in two places, it decides differently. The second argument arrived with #113: without it a DeepSeek session reaches a Qwen restore and only llama.cpp's geometry check stands in the way. THE ARGUMENT IS PART OF THE PINNED TEXT ON PURPOSE -- a surface that keeps calling this with the system prompt alone is red here, which is the only thing that catches a caller that silently stopped naming the model.
One field of the cost line, in the exact shape it is printed. cached is a statement about the prefix as it stands now, which is why it is the LAST round's figures and not a sum.

wordings.text: CUT OFF at the token budget
wordings.why: A turn cut off at the budget looks exactly like a finished one once the text stops scrolling. This is the only thing that says which of the two happened.
What Ctrl+C says. The partial turn is discarded rather than appended, and this sentence is the only place the user is told the context is untouched.
The wordmark's ground. Written once means one product; written twice means the day one of them is corrected.

The blue of the wordmark, as CROW_ACCENT_HEX writes it. Until #187 it was pinned as the truecolor escape 38;2;126;176;248, the form the terminal wrote; the window spells it in hex and the escape is gone.

wordings.text: the context went with the old server -- the next turn pays a full prefill
wordings.why: #115. The one line a switch costs, and it is said BEFORE the switch is believed rather than after -- a user who reads it once the window has emptied has been informed of a loss instead of warned about one. Two wordings would be two answers to 'where did my context go', which is the same defect the rollover note is written once for.

wordings.text: the level changes the head of every prompt -- the next turn pays a full prefill
